All these qualities should be steady in a king always; if action fails, how can a king have heaven or fame?
mahabharata:12:69.32	When a king is oppressed by a stronger king, he should call out to friends in three ways and make arrangements.
mahabharata:12:69.33	He should move the cow-camps along the roads, make villages rise and enter all of them into the branch towns.
mahabharata:12:69.34	He should enter into protected places and forts, again and again conciliating the wealthy and the chiefs of the army.
mahabharata:12:69.35	The king himself should remove the harvests; if entry is not possible, he should burn them fiercely.
mahabharata:12:69.36	With the grain in the fields, he should whisper to the enemy's men and destroy or ruin all his property by his own force.
mahabharata:12:69.37	On rivers and roads he should always destroy the crossings, drain all the water, and pollute what cannot be drained.
mahabharata:12:69.38	Disputing with the present and future about neighbouring land, counter-strikes on the enemy in battle should be made even when the time of an ally has come.
mahabharata:12:69.39	The king should have the roots of all the forts' surroundings cut, all small trees, but sparing the shrine-trees.
mahabharata:12:69.40	He should cut the branches of grown trees; but for shrine-trees it is wholly to be avoided, even the dropping of a leaf.
mahabharata:12:69.41	He should properly make parapets and openings to the sky, and fill the moats with posts, crocodiles and fish.
mahabharata:12:69.42	There should be sally-ports for the city's breathing, and their guarding, like the gates, should be done with all one's self.
mahabharata:12:69.43	At the gates he should always set heavy machines, mount shataghnis, and have them made under his own control.
mahabharata:12:69.44	Fuel should be brought in and wells dug; wells made earlier should be cleaned by those wanting water.
mahabharata:12:69.45	Houses covered with thatch should be plastered with mud, and in the month of Chaitra thatch should be removed from the city for fear of fire.
mahabharata:12:69.46	The king should have food cooked only at night; no fire should burn by day in a house except the agnihotra.
mahabharata:12:69.47	Fire should burn attentively in smithies and birth-rooms; entering houses, the fire should be controlled.
mahabharata:12:69.48	Whoever has fire by day should be given a great penalty; this should be proclaimed for the protection of the city.
mahabharata:12:69.49	Beggars, spies, drunkards, madmen and entertainers should be kept outside, best of men, otherwise they cause harm.
mahabharata:12:69.50	At crossroads, tirthas, assemblies and rest-houses, the king should post agents of fitting class everywhere.
mahabharata:12:69.51	The king should have broad royal roads made, and appoint water-sheds and shops as the place requires.
mahabharata:12:69.52	Treasuries, arsenals, granaries everywhere, stables for horses and elephants, and army offices;
mahabharata:12:69.53	moats, Kaurava, gateways and narrow passes: no one should ever see this secret, Yudhishthira.
mahabharata:12:69.54	Then a king oppressed by a strong enemy should make stores: oil, honey, ghee, grain and herbs of every kind.
mahabharata:12:69.55	He should have stores made of charcoal, kusha, munja grass, palasha, reeds, leaves, straw and fuel smeared (with ghee).
mahabharata:12:69.56	The king should make stores of all weapons—spears, lances, javelins, armour and the like.
mahabharata:12:69.57	He should especially gather all herbs, roots and fruits, and the four kinds of physicians.
mahabharata:12:69.58	Actors, dancers, wrestlers and jugglers should adorn the excellent city and entertain everywhere.
mahabharata:12:69.59	Wherever there is suspicion from a servant, a counsellor or the townsfolk, or the king's own, he should bring them under his control.
mahabharata:12:69.60	When a task is done, king of kings, he should honour them with piles of wealth, with fitting honour and with various conciliation.
mahabharata:12:69.61	Having dismissed the enemy or slain him, delight of the Kurus, the king becomes free of debt as shown in the scriptures.
mahabharata:12:69.62	A king must protect seven things; hear them from me: himself, ministers, treasury, the rod, and friends,
mahabharata:12:69.63	and the country and the city, delight of the Kurus; this sevenfold kingdom is to be protected with effort.
mahabharata:12:69.64	He who knows the six measures of policy, the triple aim and the other triad, tiger among men, enjoys this earth.
mahabharata:12:69.65	Hear what is called the six measures, Yudhishthira: making peace, sitting quiet, marching, and alliance,
mahabharata:12:69.66	waging war, sitting quiet, marching having prepared, double policy toward others, and seeking refuge with another.
mahabharata:12:69.67	And the triad that is declared—hear it here with a single mind: decline, stability and growth, and the other triad.
mahabharata:12:69.68	Dharma, wealth and desire should be followed in due time; by dharma a lord of the earth protects the earth long.
mahabharata:12:69.69	On this matter there are two verses sung by Angiras himself; blessings on you, son of the Yadavi, you ought to hear them.
mahabharata:12:69.70	Having done all tasks and rightly protected the earth, and likewise protected the townsfolk, he prospers in the next world.
mahabharata:12:69.71	What use to that king is austerity, or even sacrifices, whose subjects are all unprotected and bereft of dharma?

Hear from me the greatness of the rod-policy, as I tell it with the words of the perfected and with reasons, Bharata.
mahabharata:12:70.3	The rod-policy, rightly applied by the master, keeps the four classes to their own dharmas and restrains them from unrighteousness.
mahabharata:12:70.4	When the four classes abide in their own dharma, boundaries are not mixed, and by the rod-policy security for the subjects is made free of fear,
mahabharata:12:70.5	the three classes strive duly for soma; therefore know that the happiness of gods and men is well established.
mahabharata:12:70.6	Is the age the cause of the king, or the king the cause of the age? Let there be no doubt for you: the king is the cause of the age.
mahabharata:12:70.7	When a king acts rightly and entirely by the rod-policy, the best age, called the Krita age, sets in.
mahabharata:12:70.8	In the Krita age there is dharma, nowhere is there adharma; the minds of all classes do not delight in adharma.
mahabharata:12:70.9	Security and welfare proceed for the subjects, without doubt; Vedic rites are without fault.
mahabharata:12:70.11	Diseases do not occur here; no man is seen short-lived; widows do not occur and no cruel person is born.
mahabharata:12:70.12	The earth bears unploughed harvests, and herbs, and bark, leaves, fruits and roots are potent.
mahabharata:12:70.13	There is no adharma there, dharma alone; know these as the qualities of the Krita age, Yudhishthira.
mahabharata:12:70.14	When a king by the rod-policy follows three parts and gives up the fourth, then the Treta age begins.
mahabharata:12:70.15	Following three parts, leaving a fourth of the inauspicious; the earth is ploughed for its crops, and herbs likewise.
mahabharata:12:70.16	When the king gives up half and follows half the policy, then the age called Dvapara begins.
mahabharata:12:70.17	Then he follows two parts of the inauspicious; the earth is ploughed for crops and yields little fruit.
mahabharata:12:70.18	When a lord of the earth entirely abandons the rod-policy and troubles the subjects, entering by non-policy, then the Kali age begins.
mahabharata:12:70.19	In the Kali age there is mostly adharma and dharma is only here and there; the minds of all classes fall from their own dharma.
mahabharata:12:70.20	Shudras live by begging and Brahmanas by service; the loss of security and welfare occurs, and mixture of classes.
mahabharata:12:70.21	Vedic rites are faulty, the seasons are not pleasant, and all become sick.
mahabharata:12:70.22	The voices, colours and minds of men decline, diseases occur and people die before their span.
mahabharata:12:70.23	Widows occur and cruel offspring are born; the rain-god rains here and there, and grain grows here and there.
mahabharata:12:70.24	All savours decay when the lord of the earth does not wish to protect the subjects rightly, being devoted to the rod-policy.
mahabharata:12:70.25	The king is the maker of the Krita age, of the Treta, of the Dvapara, and of the fourth age; the king is the cause.
mahabharata:12:70.26	By making the Krita age the king attains heaven fully; by making the Treta he does not attain heaven fully.
mahabharata:12:70.27	By starting the Dvapara he obtains his portion; by starting the Kali the king incurs utter sin.
mahabharata:12:70.28	Then the evil-doer dwells in hell for eternal years, immersed in the stain of the subjects, and gains infamy and sin.
mahabharata:12:70.29	Putting the rod-policy first, a kshatriya should always desire what is not yet obtained and protect what is obtained.
mahabharata:12:70.30	The rod-policy rightly applied is the boundary-maker of the world, its limit, and its sustainer, like mother and father.
mahabharata:12:70.31	Know that in which beings come to be, bull of the Bharatas: this alone is the supreme dharma, that a king be possessed of the rod-policy.
mahabharata:12:70.32	Therefore, Kaurava, protect the subjects by dharma, with policy; conducting yourself so, protecting the subjects, you will win heaven, hard to win.

This is a list of thirty-six qualities, joined to thirty-six qualities; one endowed with qualities who practises the qualities will gain virtue.
mahabharata:12:71.3	He should practise dharma without harshness, give up affection without being an unbeliever, practise wealth without cruelty, and pursue desire without arrogance.
mahabharata:12:71.4	He should speak pleasantly without meanness, be brave without boasting, give but not rain on the unworthy, be bold but not harsh.
mahabharata:12:71.5	He should make peace but not with the ignoble, not quarrel with kinsmen, not employ spies who are strangers, and do his work without oppression.
mahabharata:12:71.6	He should not speak of his aims to the wicked, nor speak of his own merits, nor take from the good, nor rely on a bad man.
mahabharata:12:71.7	He should not apply the rod without examination, nor reveal counsel, nor release to the greedy, nor trust wrongdoers.
mahabharata:12:71.8	Free of jealousy, guarding his wives, pure, a king should be unmerciful where needed; he should not indulge too much with a woman, nor eat the over-refined or the unwholesome.
mahabharata:12:71.9	Not stiff, he should honour the worthy, serve teachers without deceit, worship the gods without hypocrisy, and desire blameless prosperity.
mahabharata:12:71.11	He should not strike without knowing, nor leave a remnant of slain foes; he should not be angry for no reason, and be gentle toward wrongdoers.
mahabharata:12:71.12	Act thus, abiding in kingship, if you wish good here; otherwise a king meets supreme fear.
mahabharata:12:71.13	He who follows all these qualities as stated, having enjoyed good things here, is honoured in heaven after death.
Hearing this speech of Shantanu's son, Yudhishthira, surrounded by the chief Pandavas, then bowed to the grandsire, and the wise king did as said.

I shall briefly tell you, dear one, the settled dharmas; in detail one could never reach the end of dharmas.
mahabharata:12:72.3	You should lodge in your house honoured twice-born, virtuous, devoted to dharma, learned, and steadfast in Vedic vows.
mahabharata:12:72.4	Rising to meet them, clasping and saluting their feet, you should do all your tasks with your household priest.
mahabharata:12:72.5	Having completed the duties of dharma and performed auspicious rites, you should have Brahmanas pronounce blessings of success and victory.
mahabharata:12:72.6	Endowed with uprightness, steadiness and wisdom, Bharata, one should gather wealth for wealth's sake and avoid desire and anger.
mahabharata:12:72.7	A king who pursues wealth putting desire and anger first gains neither dharma nor wealth, the foolish one.
mahabharata:12:72.8	Do not appoint greedy or foolish men to matters of desire and wealth; appoint the ungreedy and wise in all works.
mahabharata:12:72.9	A fool appointed to matters of wealth, unskilled in affairs, troubles the subjects by mismanagement, joined to desire and aversion.
mahabharata:12:72.12	People are devoted to one who protects, gives, is ever devoted to dharma, untiring, and free of desire and aversion.
mahabharata:12:72.13	Do not seek to gain wealth by unrighteous profit; for the dharma and wealth of him who goes against the scriptures are unstable.
mahabharata:12:72.14	A king who goes against the scriptures does not accumulate; his wealth, out of place, all perishes.
mahabharata:12:72.15	One who, rooted in wealth, does violence to himself, oppressing the subjects through delusion by taxes not seen in the scriptures,
mahabharata:12:72.16	is like one who cuts off the udder of a cow wishing milk and gets no milk; so a kingdom oppressed by mismanagement does not prosper.
mahabharata:12:72.17	One who attends the milch cow always gets milk; so a kingdom enjoyed by proper means yields fruit.
mahabharata:12:72.18	Then a kingdom enjoyed by proper means and well protected ever brings an unequalled increase of the treasury, Yudhishthira.
mahabharata:12:72.19	The subjects, well protected by the king, yield grain and gold, always satisfied from their own and others', as a mother her milk.
mahabharata:12:72.20	Be like a garland-maker, O king, not a charcoal-burner; so yoked you can enjoy the kingdom long, protecting it.
mahabharata:12:72.21	If you lose wealth through an enemy's attack, then seek by conciliation alone the wealth that is not Brahmanas'.
mahabharata:12:72.22	Do not let your mind be moved on seeing a Brahmana's wealth, even in the last extremity, how much less in prosperity, Bharata.
mahabharata:12:72.23	Give them wealth as you are able and as they deserve; conciliating and protecting, you will gain heaven, hard to win.
mahabharata:12:72.24	Thus protecting the subjects by dharma and right conduct, you will gain good, merit and fame, delight of the Kurus.
mahabharata:12:72.25	Protect the subjects with dharma and right dealing, Pandava; so yoked, Yudhishthira, you will not be bound by fetters.
mahabharata:12:72.26	This alone is the supreme dharma, that a king protect his subjects; protection of beings in dharma is supreme compassion.
mahabharata:12:72.27	Therefore the knowers of dharma hold this the supreme dharma: that a king devoted to protection shows compassion to beings.
mahabharata:12:72.28	The sin a king does in a day, failing to protect the subjects out of fear, he reaches its end after a thousand years.
mahabharata:12:72.29	The merit he does in a day, protecting the subjects by dharma, he enjoys the fruit of in heaven for ten thousand years.
mahabharata:12:72.30	As many worlds as one conquers by good sacrifice, good study and good austerity, so many he attains in a moment, protecting the subjects by dharma.
mahabharata:12:72.31	Thus protecting dharma with effort, son of Kunti, having obtained fruit of merit here, you will not be bound by fetters.
mahabharata:12:72.32	And in the world of heaven you will gain great fortune, Pandava; such dharmas do not arise in the kingless; therefore there is no one but the king who can obtain great fruit.
mahabharata:12:72.33	Having obtained a prosperous kingdom and protecting it by dharma, satisfy Indra with soma and friends and people with their desires.

Here too they tell this ancient history, the dialogue of Pururavas, son of Ila, with Matarishvan (Wind).
mahabharata:12:73.3	Whence is the Brahmana born, and whence the other three classes, and by what is one better? Tell me this, Wind."

The Brahmana, best of kings, was created from Brahma's mouth, the kshatriya from the arms, and the Vaishya is said to be from the thighs.
mahabharata:12:73.5	For the service of the three classes, bull among men, a fourth class, the Shudra, was afterward formed from the feet.
mahabharata:12:73.6	The Brahmana, as soon as born, was born to the earth as lord of all beings, for the guarding of the treasury of dharma.
mahabharata:12:73.7	Then he made the second class, the kshatriya, the earth's protector and rod-bearer, for the protection of subjects.
mahabharata:12:73.8	The Vaishya should support these three classes with wealth and grain, and the Shudra should serve them—so is Brahma's command.
To whom does this earth belong, by dharma, together with its wealth, to the twice-born or the kshatriya? Tell me rightly, Wind.

The Brahmana eats his own, wears his own, and gives his own; the teacher is the eldest and best of all classes, the twice-born.
mahabharata:12:73.12	As, in the absence of a husband, a woman takes the brother-in-law as husband, so the kshatriya, as the next, takes the earth as husband.
mahabharata:12:73.13	This is the first rule for you; in calamity there may be another, if you seek the highest station in heaven by dharma.
mahabharata:12:73.14	Whoever conquers the land should present it to a Brahmana endowed with learning and conduct, knowing dharma, an ascetic,
mahabharata:12:73.15	content with his own dharma, who is not intent on wealth, who leads the king by wisdom wholly filled.
mahabharata:12:73.16	A Brahmana born in a family, of trained understanding and gentle speech, leads the king to the good, speaking the wondrous Sarasvati (speech).
mahabharata:12:73.17	The dharma that a king practises, as shown by a Brahmana, obedient, without self-assertion, established in the vow of kshatriya dharma,
mahabharata:12:73.18	by that he of trained mind stays long in fame; the king's priest is a sharer in all that dharma.
mahabharata:12:73.19	Thus all subjects who rely on the king, rightly conducted, abiding in their own dharma, are afraid of nothing.
mahabharata:12:73.20	The dharma which they practise in the kingdom, well protected by the king—a fourth part of that dharma the king obtains.
mahabharata:12:73.21	Gods, men, ancestors, Gandharvas, serpents and Rakshasas live by sacrifice; there is no sacrifice in a kingless realm.
mahabharata:12:73.22	Gods and ancestors live by what is given from here; the security and welfare of this dharma rest on the king.
mahabharata:12:73.23	One finds comfort in shade, in water, in wind when hot; one finds comfort in fire, in a garment, in the sun when cold.
mahabharata:12:73.24	The mind delights in sound, touch, taste, form and smell; in all those pleasures one afraid gains no happiness.
mahabharata:12:73.25	He who gives fearlessness gains a very great fruit; for there is no gift equal to life in the three worlds.
mahabharata:12:73.26	The king is Indra, the king is Yama, the king is Dharma too; the king bears forms; by the king all this is upheld.

Of those kings whose priest is righteous and knows dharma, and who are themselves of such quality, all is well with them.
mahabharata:12:74.3	Both make the subjects prosper and the gods, earlier and later ancestors, when the two stand together in dharma, trusted and of great austerity.
mahabharata:12:74.4	As friends of each other, honoured, of equal mind, by the honour of Brahma and kshatriya the subjects gain happiness.
mahabharata:12:74.5	By dishonouring them the subjects would perish; Brahmana and kshatriya together are called the root of all dharmas.
mahabharata:12:74.6	Here too they recite this ancient history; hear it, Yudhishthira, the dialogue of Aila and Kashyapa.
mahabharata:12:74.7	When the Brahmana abandons the kshatriya, or the kshatriya abandons the Brahmana, whom do those who follow strength follow, and whom do the weak leave?
mahabharata:12:74.8	The kingdom of the kshatriya is ruined where Brahmana and kshatriya are in conflict; there robbers take hold of the strong and the good depart with weakness.
mahabharata:12:74.9	Their bulls do not grow nor do their cows give milk, the churns are not churned, they do not sacrifice, their sons do not study the Veda, when Brahmanas and kshatriyas forsake each other.
mahabharata:12:74.14	The Brahmana is a tree; guarded, it rains honey and gold; unguarded it rains constant tears and sin.
mahabharata:12:74.15	When a non-celibate has fallen from conduct, and one Brahmana seeks protection of another, the god sends marvellous rain, and unbearable (evils) enter again and again.
mahabharata:12:74.16	Where a sinner, having killed a woman or a Brahmana, gets praise in an assembly and does not fear in the king's presence, there fear arises for the kshatriya.
mahabharata:12:74.17	When sinners commit sin beyond measure, then the god Rudra is born; by sinners sinners create Rudra, who then strikes all, good and bad.
mahabharata:12:74.18	Whence is Rudra, and what kind is Rudra? Beings are seen to be slain by beings; tell me this, learned Kashyapa, from whence this god Rudra is born.
mahabharata:12:74.19	The self, Rudra, in the heart of men, slays each one's own body and another's; they call Rudra like wind and tempest, his form like forest fires and clouds.
mahabharata:12:74.20	No one holds back the wind, the cloud does not rain, nor does the fire; so yoked he is seen in men, bound and freed by desire and aversion.
mahabharata:12:74.21	As fire blazing in one house, swift, may burn a whole village, so this god makes bewilderment, and then all is touched by merit and sin.
mahabharata:12:74.22	If the rod touches one who has merit when sinners commit sin without distinction, then for what reason should one do good, or for what reason not do evil?
mahabharata:12:74.23	Because sinners are not abandoned, equal punishment touches the sinless by mixture; the wet burns with the dry through mixing; let there be no mixing with sinners in any way.
mahabharata:12:74.24	The earth bears the good and the bad; the sun warms the good and the bad; the wind blows on the good and the bad; and waters carry the good and the bad.
mahabharata:12:74.25	So it goes in this world, but not so in the next, prince; after death there is a great difference between the two, between him who does merit and him who does sin.
mahabharata:12:74.26	The world of merit is honeyed, with flames of ghee, golden light, the navel of nectar; there the celibate rejoices after death; there is neither death nor old age nor sorrow.
mahabharata:12:74.27	The world of sin is a hell, dark, ever painful, full of grief; there the sinner grieves for himself, falling for many years without foothold.
mahabharata:12:74.28	By mutual division of Brahmanas and kshatriyas, the subjects enter unbearable sorrow; knowing this, a wise king should make his priest learned in more than one science.
mahabharata:12:74.29	Let him be consecrated; so dharma is ordained; for the Brahmana is called the foremost of all here by dharma.
mahabharata:12:74.30	Brahmanas were created first, so the knowers of dharma know; by his eldest lineage all the later has been obtained.
mahabharata:12:74.31	Therefore the Brahmana is to be honoured and revered, enjoying the first portion; everything best and highest is to be offered to him by dharma.
mahabharata:12:74.32	This must necessarily be done by a king, even a strong one; Brahma makes the kshatriya grow, and from the kshatriya Brahma grows.

The Brahmana calms the subjects' fear seen and unseen, and the king by his arms; so that kingdom prospers in happiness.
mahabharata:12:75.3	Here too they recite this ancient history, the dialogue of King Muchukunda with Vaishravana.
mahabharata:12:75.4	Muchukunda, lord of the earth, having conquered this earth, wishing to test his own strength, went against the lord of Alaka.
mahabharata:12:75.5	Then King Vaishravana sent forth Rakshasas; those Nairritas crushed his forces as they advanced.
mahabharata:12:75.6	As his army was being slain, King Muchukunda, subduer of foes, reproached his learned priest.
mahabharata:12:75.7	Then Vasishtha, best of Brahma-knowers, practised fierce austerity, slew the Rakshasas there, and found a path.
[Bhishma said:] Then Time approached concerning that doubt of dharma and wealth, and said to the serpent, Death and the greedy Arjunaka:
The eldest of them was Vimshati, matching the archers; and Vimshati's son was auspicious Vivimshati, Bharata.
I who consecrated the evil-minded, foolish Duryodhana as ruler of the Kauravas, increaser of the fear of kinsmen...
Then in the midst of the assembly Yuyudhana, mad with drink, said to Kritavarman, laughing and scorning:
[Yudhishthira said:] "You ate too much and boasted of your life, Partha, without regard for another; therefore you are fallen on the ground."
Told so, they all spoke on every side: "I am Karna, I am Bhimasena, I am Arjuna," lord.
